title: Steve Kaczynski & Scott Duke Kominers | The Everything Token | Talks at Google
description:
Steve Kaczynski & Scott Duke Kominers discuss their book The Everything Token: How NFTs and Web3 Will Transform the Way We Buy, Sell, and Create, a guide that explains why NFTs are valuable, and how businesses can leverage them to build engaged, intensely loyal communities around their products and brands.

Get the book here: https://goo.gle/3vDER79

Steve Kaczynski is a communications and marketing professional with 15+ years of experience, including stints in leadership at Progressive Insurance and Nestle. 

Scott Duke Kominers is the Sarofim-Rock Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School and a research partner at a16z crypto. He co-leads Harvard’s Crypto, Fintech, and Web3 Lab. 

Both advise entrepreneurs and established firms on NFTs, web3, and marketplace design, and are avid NFT collectors and creators themselves.

Moderated by Karim Salamah.

#nft
summary: Steve Kaczynski and Scott Duke Kominers discuss their backgrounds and motivations for researching NFTs and Web3, noting that Kaczynski was inspired by the potential of smart contracts and loyalty rewards while Kominers was drawn to the unique market design and community formation of NFTs. They explain that their book, 'The Everything Token,' explores how these technologies transform buying, selling, and creating across various industries such as loyalty programs and ticketing.

transcript: [MUSIC PLAYING] KARIM SALAMA: Good morning, everyone. My name is Karim Salama, and I'm so excited that I have the opportunity to interview and learn more about NFTs and Web3. I'm joined today by Steve Kaczynski and Scott Duke Kominers. Steve and Scott are here to talk with us about their book "The Everything Token-- How NFTs and Web3 Will Transform the Way We Buy, Sell, and Create." Steve Kaczynski is a communications and marketing professional with 15 plus years of experience, including stints in leadership at Progressive Insurance and Nestle. And Scott Duke Kominers Is the Sarofim-Rock Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School and a research partner at A16 Crypto. He co-leads Harvard's Crypto Fintech and Web3 lab. So welcome to you both. Thank you for the time. If we could [INAUDIBLE] of course. SCOTT KOMINERS: Thanks so much. Thanks for having us. KARIM SALAMA: If we could jump right into it, my first question to both of you is what drew each of you to research about NFTs and Web3? STEVE KACZYNSKI: I mean, I can start. And my background-- it's funny. I always tell people it actually started in the mid '90s, which makes absolutely no sense until you have the context of that is sort of my background. I've always been interested in tech. And when I was in middle school in '95, '96, I was coding websites and actually creating HTML websites, obviously before the days of Google, who we're talking to right here. And so those resources weren't quite as available. But I always found it was fascinating that I could code something, and someone in Paris, France would see the same thing by putting in the address. And of course, that was super interesting. And similarly, I was early to Facebook in 2004 and and X now, at the time Twitter in 2009, crypto in the 2017, 2018 time frame. So for me, I've always been super interested in tech. And I remember when I discovered NFTs, it was sort of this click moment for me, because obviously, we'll get deeper into the subject of the book and what that is, but effectively, I was, in 2018, telling my poor team at Progressive, anybody who would listen to me, that I thought the Ethereum blockchain was brilliant for creating these smart contracts where you could build businesses. Now, the applications hadn't been built out yet, so in 2020, 2021 time frame when I learned that people were starting to do this, I dug in and wanted to learn everything I can, and, of course, then ended up meeting Scott. And within about nine months, we co-authored the first "Harvard Business Review" article about NFTs together. So for me, it's just a passion of tech, a passion of new markets, a passion of human behavior, and kind of putting all those things in one was something that got me really inspired. SCOTT KOMINERS: And first of all, a lot of similarities and correlates. I, too, was coding websites. And I remember when that Google thing appeared. It was like, oh, this is like, the coolest thing I've ever seen. And I got to say, it was even cooler when I learned about the PageRank algorithm, right? I've been someone who's been studying marketplace design and the intersections of computer science and economics and mathematics to make markets work better now since college. And at HBS, I built our course curriculum on marketplaces. It's called Making Markets. And in the context of all of that work, sort of as a scholar of market design, I've, of course, been very aware of crypto in many different contexts. But what I really-- I hadn't grokked, right? Lots of people talk about cryptocurrency. Currencies are actually very hard to make use of as mediums of exchange for a long time, because a currency can't be used for lots of different purposes until many different people are willing to accept it in exchange for goods and services. It actually takes a long time to get started. NFTs, by contrast-- and I wrote an article that pointed this out with Christian Catalini and Ravi Jagadeesan in early 2021-- start from a small, close-knit community of enthusiasts and spin outwards, right? They can gain value immediately because a small set of people all agree like, this thing is valuable. This thing has meaning to me. And so I'd written that in theory, but even so, I think I still hadn't really completely understood it until, in the summer of 2021, hilariously, I'd written a puzzle. I'm a semi-professional puzzle-writer on the side. I was writing a puzzle column for "Bloomberg Opinion" at the time. I wrote a puzzle about NFTs, and a bunch of people from NFT world saw it and wrote to me and were like, look, you seem like you would get it. You should come and join one of our NFT communities, and come and experience this space. And I showed up, and I discovered that there were so many new types of transactions and community formation around this sort of new market design primitive that I had never really understood before. And I'm like oh my gosh, I have to be able to teach this in my class in like, six months, and I know almost nothing. And so as a scholar, this is like, the most fascinating position you can be in, but it's also a little terrifying because you now have a fuse. You've got to understand the thing well enough not just to be able to write about it, but to be able to teach it to students, and you've got six months. It was really, really lucky to meet Steve, and he's been the most incredible thought partner on this whole journey. KARIM SALAMA: That's awesome. Thank you so much for telling us a little bit about your backgrounds. I mean, since you both come from pretty different places and came into this space, I was wondering, can you share interests about your particular areas of interest within the NFT and Web3 space? STEVE KACZYNSKI: I mean, just to even take a higher level at that, it's funny because we obviously have our more niche interests, and I'll get into those too. But it's funny because the title of the book actually is because-- the funny story about the title of the book, which we actually write about in there, is our editor and our publisher was basically saying, hey, if we're writing the title to be straightforward about a complex topic, what problem do NFTs solve? And we started saying, well, you know, it's loyalty rewards and ticketing and brand-building, and we started listing all these things. We're like credentials, and we're like, it's kind of everything in every industry. So there's all these different ones that they can potentially affect. Now, for me, one of the ones that interests me in particular is the concept of loyalty rewards. I happen to work as the community lead with Starbucks on Starbucks Odyssey, which is their next-generation loyalty program that they're beta testing in Web3 right now. And the way that they use loyalty rewards to make it sort of a two-way interaction, where previously, you buy something, you can get a reward, you then exchange that reward to get a product or whatever. But now it's like they can do all sorts of brand-building missions where you learn about the brand. Maybe take a virtual tour of a roastery, and then maybe you buy a certain product, and you get a stamp, which has points. And those can correlate to levels of loyalty, which manifest in rewards. There's a special tumbler behind me that you can see, a pumpkin spice latte tumbler or a tumbler with one of my NFTs on it. Or you can sell those stamps to somebody else who wants to get more points to acquire those rewards. So that two-way loyalty may seem small, but it makes a huge difference to the consumer in becoming a superfan because they engage with the brand more. It's not simply purchase and make it as transactional, but instead developing a relationship with the brand. And many brands have the opportunity to use Web3 as a better set of crypto rails to do that and a better set of overall software rails from an NFT perspective. So for me, loyalty rewards, and then ticketing, which I won't go deep into, because I know I gave a really long example there. But ticketing is the other one that's super interesting to me, but I'll hand it over to Scott to see what his interests are. SCOTT KOMINERS: Totally fine. I can take ticketing. So for me as a scholar of market design, I'm always fascinated by technologies that enable new types of transactions or improvements to existing transaction contexts. And one of the things that puzzles people a lot about the early NFT market is that a lot of the early applications were things we might think of as like, digital collectibles, whether they're digital trading cards or artworks or something of the sort. But there are all these digital images or media files, and you sort of wonder why is that? This is super strange. What an unusual application for a market. But in fact, there are lots of digital collectibles that have existed before, and similarly like digital files. Think of your music stored in iTunes or your Kindle books, your ebooks in Amazon or something of the sort. But they've always lived inside of a single platform. The reason for that is that you've needed a platform wrapper to try and determine provenance and to make sure the acid is unique or individually scarce. And why is that? Well, think about the alternate context in which you're just like an artist selling a digital image. If you show someone the image to give them the option to buy it, you're basically giving them a copy of it, right? They can just save it on their computer, and now they've got it. And that's why you have watermarks on places like Getty Images. NFTs solve this problem. They provide a digital record of ownership that can be attached to other media, digital or physical even. And it serves sort of a digital deed. It's a way to manage a transaction and define a unique owner over a data record, a piece of media, or something of the sort. And we now know that, for example-- and it does it without any intermediary, right? The [INAUDIBLE] exists without a platform. It's as if your Pokemon could exist independent of Pokemon Go. And so that even if the platform shut down, if, God forbid, whatever music streaming and collection service you're using shuts down, your music collection would just vanish. With NFTs, the music persists even beyond the platform, and you can take it to whatever player you want like you would with a CD or cassette or something even more legacy. But once you realize that digital asset primitive, there are lots of other digital asset transactions we engage in which this can make better, and the tickets is a prime example. Because if you think about what is a digital ticket today? It's like a QR code in your email. If you're going to buy a ticket to a sold out show, like you're trying to get a secondary market Hamilton ticket because you happen to be in New York, you have to trust that someone is selling you the ticket uniquely, right? Because they forward you the QR code. What's to stop them from using it or selling it, too, or selling it to three other people? With an NFT, there's a unique asset. And you can actually use a software process to bind the transfer of the asset and the transfer of the payment into a single software process. So if it completes, you know the payment went to the seller, and the ticket went to you. And once you control the ticket, the seller can't anymore, and can't give it to anyone else. And so you can do that secure exchange without any sort of intermediary platform. And again, the asset itself exists independent of a platform, and this is just fascinating to me. There's so many digital markets where a better ownership primitive is a really powerful tool. KARIM SALAMA: That's all great, and it was actually getting to one of my next questions as I think about it. So you've mentioned several use cases for NFTs. You mentioned corporate loyalty rewards programs. You've also mentioned the ticketing. I'm wondering if we could just take a step back, and you're talking to a beginner. I'll put myself out there. As someone who's never bought trading cards, art, and is not much of a collector, how would you explain the value of an NFT to somebody like that? SCOTT KOMINERS: Great. OK, so first, we should think a little bit about the design paradigm that goes on in Web3. So it's a different model of the way you interface on the internet, and the central object is what's often called a digital wallet. It's a core identity. It's an account for you that you control-- you have unique control over your wallet-- and you can bring from across platforms. So you go to a website. You connect your wallet. It's actually a little bit like login with Google or something of the sort. When you connect login with Google, it transfers a bunch of your profile information. The website can maybe see your profile picture and imports your email address and maybe your phone number or something of the sort. This is that, but it's like your own private repository that holds all of your digital assets, and you can use it flexibly anywhere. You connect to a given application, you connect your wallet, and the wallet reads all the assets in that identity and can respond to them. And so first of all, that means you can have an identity that's fundamentally cross-platform. So like in your social media experience, you might have a LinkedIn and a Twitter and maybe an Instagram. And you spend a lot of time uploading the same content to both, but even more, you might have a follow graph on one that's really hard to transport to another. And you just want to get your friends, bring your Instagram friends also to your Twitter feed or whatever, and that's really, really hard. In a Web3 world, that's automatic because your follow graph is part of your core digital identity. And all the platforms that you connect to read parts of it or read whatever part you share with them. And so now, if you're a content creator, you can build up an audience and take that audience with you from platform to platform. And even more crucially, you can cross-integrate the experience on many different platforms. Your YouTube content and your Twitter content can coexist, and you sort of co-create a more valuable product for everyone. The other thing, maybe one other simple example that we often give, is what we call multithreaded subscriptions. So maybe you really want to read all the news about your local sports team. And so because of that, you subscribe to the local newspaper because they cover your sports team, of course. But a critical problem here is that half the team games are away, and that means that there is a lot of really good content about them in other local newspapers, and it's other local newspapers everywhere. You can't just subscribe to one other city's news, because your team is playing all across the country, maybe the world. You could imagine an NFT that represents-- and maybe you even get it from the team. It doesn't come from one of the newspapers. It's a unified subscription to all news about your team, and it lives in your digital wallet. And when you get up in the morning, you just go to whatever news site wherever they played. You go to that news site, you connect your wallet. It sees that you have this all-access subscription to the team, unlocks the articles, lets you through the paywall. And then meanwhile, the team subsidizes. And so it enables these new economies with third-party value creation in a way that [INTERPOSING VOICES] STEVE KACZYNSKI: And if I can back it up even further than that, for a lot of people, they might be saying, what is an NFT in the first place? In which case, one of the things that I even go to-- and I know we talked about the establishment of digital property rights. But one of our mutual friends goes by the name of Adam Hollander, who he has this thing we call the Hollander explanation, which is imagine you go into a museum, and you see a beautiful painting on the wall. You can take a picture of that painting, but that picture is not worth really anything, right? It's just in your phone. You can buy a print in the gift shop of that painting, but it's also not worth much more than the paper it's printed on. The reason why the one on the wall is worth so much money is because the museum owns it, it's the original, and they can prove both of those things. And it's a simple way to explain that that digital ownership then leads to that flexibility that Scott was mentioning, where, again, using a very practical example for a company, especially if someone's building against it, let's say you have a certain video game skin, and it's an NFT. Instead of living in that walled garden, you have a Fortnite skin. I used to work with Hot Pockets at Nestle. They sponsored NRG, which is a gaming team. To nobody's surprise, gamers overlapped well with Hot Pocket eaters. That is who they're trying to market to, right? But it's a very broad appeal, right? Going in. Not that they wouldn't still do that. They certainly would. But you could also say everybody who owns a certain Fortnite skin can connect their digital wallet that Scott was talking about, and just basically by connecting that wallet, get a 25% discount off their new product. Now, suddenly, you have a very precise idea that this is absolutely our target market. We are absolutely getting in there. And it's a win for both the gamer, and sometimes, the gamer, if they're younger, a win for the parent who's doing it, too, saying, my kid's helping me save on my groceries. The kid is getting the Hot Pockets, and now suddenly, you have someone in your ecosystem who otherwise might not be, and you can target your fans. I mean, right now, Drake or Mr. Beast, they don't know who their top fans are. NFTs allow you to precisely see that as a company. And then to even expand a little bit further on the question, we use the term "NFTs" a lot. It very well is probably going to be like mp3s. In the early 2000s, everyone talked about mp3's and whatever, but no one says mp3s. It's just music. No one says QR code. No one says, "Let me go to the baseball game and grab my QR code." You grab your ticket. NFTs will very likely be the thing or the program that enables it. And I think for most people, for consumers, they're not going to know that they're interacting with NFTs or the blockchain. It's just going to work, just as we don't care if something's on a certain type of Cloud service. If it works, we care that it works. So it will be the software that flexibly powers those things, I think. SCOTT KOMINERS: And sorry, if I can cut it back in for one more second, it's going to power a different type of brand experience, right? So NFTs, again, because they're these cross-platform-- we say interoperable. They can interoperate across many different platforms. They're these cross-platform assets, and the ones on public blockchains, at least, are also publicly visible. They, in effect, take everyone who owns the product and unify them into a network. It takes all of the people in a brand, all of a brand's enthusiasts, and turns them into a network that can together build the brand in value, and is, to some degree, directly incentivized to do so because they're owners. And if you think about it, this is something brands have been trying to do forever. If you're a clothing company, you would love to have an ongoing interaction with your customer in their experience of owning their clothing and wearing it around and wearing it to major sporting events or to the theater or whatever. But you can't do that as a clothing company because you have no direct connection to the customer once they own the asset, once they purchase the asset. Or you maybe work really hard at it. You have an email list, and you have to get them to show up. Or you have an Instagram feed, and you want them to post, but it's really hard. And moreover, someone who's a fan-- as Steve says, if you're a big Fortnite player, there's a lot of other stuff you might be a fan of. And you might have friends or you'll be friends with people who are also fans, but it's hard to find them. The NFT overlays a network onto all of those consumer experiences and means that you can be in bidirectional ongoing communication with the brand and find and form a community around the brand sort of unifying all of the enthusiasts. KARIM SALAMA: Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. It starts to raise a question, given how much opportunity there is for it to be used, to me about the value and how do you find the value of an NFT, or the actual price of it. So what elements or factors do you think influence the price of an NFT? STEVE KACZYNSKI: This is one of those interesting ones where, to me, it's funny. I actually go back to-- because there are certainly NFTs that have the speculative values that go up. And as any early market, you see this happening, right? We saw it with the early dot-com boom. We see it throughout tech markets or markets where there's financial incentives. That said, to me, I would actually take a different lens on that and say, what is the value to the individual user as it relates to the business? So for example, if I don't wear Nike shoes, it doesn't make sense for me to go spend a bunch of money on Nike NFTs, because the utility associated with them and what Nike is going to program against them is going to be related to Nike shoes. Now, I do wear Nike shoes, so I do own Nike NFTs, and I own Adidas NFT because I do all the same there too. But if there's brands that I don't interact with-- I've had conversations with people related to the Starbucks work I do, which is people will be like, oh, I don't really drink coffee, but I'm interested in these Starbucks NFTs. It's like, well, if you don't drink coffee or engage with Starbucks, then a loyalty program-- sure, you could sign up, and you could participate, but you're not going to get the maximum value out of it. So to me, I tend to look at it a little bit different, where yes, there are things that can certainly affect the price of NFTs. They can go up and down. But I think what interests us more than that, or at least me personally-- I don't want to speak for Scott-- is the brand-building dynamics that they can be used for, because I think they can fundamentally create these aligned incentive structures between consumers and businesses, and they can fundamentally change the way that we interact with other fans of the brand so you can find your tribe everywhere. I mean, you think about Jeep people, for example. People love their Jeeps. Love their Jeeps, right? And so it's like, imagine if somebody who owns a Jeep in California can become friends with someone who owns a Jeep in North Mantako, Minnesota or Montgomery, Alabama simply because they have an NFT that allows them to get access to a digital space. We have seen this with Starbucks, where people in California and Washington are great friends with people in Chicago and New York and LA and all these other places that they never would have met had not they owned this NFT and have the ability to connect. So not to completely dodge that question, but I think the interest we have is actually less in the financialization of it and more in the opportunity it presents to create really robust brands and really robust utility for customers and brands alike. SCOTT KOMINERS: Totally agreed. And I should say, by the way, talking about people who would never have met without NFTs, Steve and I met, of course, entirely through NFT world in a live Twitter space for an NFT community we were both in. And we talk about this in the book. To this date, we've never actually met in person. We've spent thousands of hours on calls together. We wrote a book together and a bunch of articles, and we have never actually met face to face. It's a very Web3, internet-enabled interaction. But yeah, so another thing we talk about is that really, truly, we think that the ubiquity of NFTs is going to come from lots of these little micro applications that are very broad mass-market. It's digital tickets. It's coffee rewards. It's souvenir stamps when you visit a national park. Lots of these things are going to be sold in massive quantities for like, a dollar or as freebies when you do a thing, just as sort of a reward for coming. You went to the national park, you took some photos, and you collected your stamp, just like we have stamp passports for national parks today. So we think the opportunity is mostly around these broadly accessible, consumer-facing NFT products. By the way, not even just collectibles or tradable items, but also identity records of various forms, like credentials from online courses. Maybe even one day with the proper privacy guardrails in place, your health data, making it much easier to move your dental records from one provider to another than it is today, where you have to call someone, do a bunch of authorizations, get the thing faxed, then fax it to somebody else. Who even has a fax machine today? This could all just be completely seamless through your digital wallet. And so price is just going to be like ordinary goods, right? It's going to be prices determined by the value to the consumer. And then the total value that these types of consumer experiences can create is going to be much greater than digital [INAUDIBLE] STEVE KACZYNSKI: And one last thing. I just want to build on that from a community-building perspective because Scott brought it up really well, is that people hear our story that we've never met in person. We wrote a book together, we wrote articles together, and they say, wow, that's crazy. I think our type of story will be entirely more common in the next 7 to 10 years as this continues to grow from a brand-building perspective, because people can do that. And the opportunity to connect in those digital spaces-- I mean, before I got into Web3, even before COVID, it was rare that I would see and hang out with friends quite as often. But now that I have access to these digital spaces based on what I own, where my interests are, I have more friends and more discussions and feel more socially connected than ever before in my life. SCOTT KOMINERS: Absolutely. STEVE KACZYNSKI: And I think it's something that humans are craving more because they're so busy as it is. We're spending more time online in digital spaces. And so I think being able to connect in digital spaces with people who have the same passion, whether you're an Ohio State Buckeye fan, or whether you are somebody who is passionate about your Harley-Davidson motorcycle, the chance to really connect in those niche communities, I think, is going to expand like crazy. SCOTT KOMINERS: Totally. KARIM SALAMA: Yeah. That makes a lot of sense. I can think about how a lot of those traditional communities you mentioned, like the Jeep community or your college community, would bond. One of my questions is what are some of the most creative kind of communities or maybe corporate partnerships you've seen that have helped build community? STEVE KACZYNSKI: I mean, we've mentioned Starbucks and Nike off the bat. I do want to give credit to Adidas because I think they came in really smart early on, where in order to introduce some new merchandise in a gated drop, which, by the way, very logical business case for them, right? If Adidas drops merchandise, and it can sometimes get [INAUDIBLE],, well, why not have a gated drop for your true fans to be able to get access to buy without any sort of pressure or issues? And they partnered with a couple of the Bored Ape Yacht Club, which is one of the really popular clubs run by Yuga Labs, a startup that got $450 million in funding as a unicorn startup. They partnered with Pixel Vault, which is sort of a decentralized gaming network now that they work on. And they were really smart in that partnership because it meant that everything would work. They didn't come in and just try to do things in an inauthentic way. They were able to engage with the community, a couple of communities that worked really well. And they were able to then ultimately gate their drop and ensure that their tech worked really well. So I like that one as well. But that one comes to mind for me, as well as, again, Nike and Starbucks, I think, are crushing it. SCOTT KOMINERS: So first of all, agreed on all of those. I think also important to emphasize-- you mentioned Bored Ape Yacht Club, Steve. There are a number of digitally native brands that have built off of NFTs as a springboard into broader and more complex brand activations, and even physical products. There's this company, Pudgy Penguins, for example, that started with NFTs to build an initial community of enthusiasts-- and many others have actually done this, too, like Kitaro Studios, like others-- and then now are selling physical products in the world that also come with NFTs attached. And so their initial fan base around the NFTs then creates a springboard with which to build a fan base around the physical assets, which then brings more people into the NFT space. I also think there's a lot of fascinating stuff going on with transmedia. For example, there's a media studio called Forgotten Runes that created a series of NFT characters-- think your Dungeons and Dragons-type wizards and stuff-- and then people in the community created stories around their wizards and history and structure for them, which then the brand integrated a lot of those into a comics series and a couple of video games. And there's this-- Steve and I call it in the book, a semi-permeable membrane between the canon and the fandom, and you can imagine that for lots of other media properties. Think sort of the "Star Wars" of the world. And then I guess the other thing to really call out is that we're seeing more and more emerging applications, right? And it's almost impossible to guess right now what will be the most exciting NFTs in five years, because conceptually, it's a new technology. It's like the early days of the internet all over again. But for example, right now something people are thinking really hard about is using NFTs to do cross-platform identity records for people that prove they are who they say they are. In a world that's becoming more concerned about AI fakes, now having a digital signature that proves you are who you say you are-- you go to a human, you present ID, you get authenticated, but then you get a digital asset that you control, that you can use to sign things as this is me-- I think that type of application is going to be very relevant very soon. KARIM SALAMA: You beat me to my next question, because that's actually what I was thinking of. You've mentioned so many limitless kind of opportunities to get involved in this space. But if I could ask each of you maybe just one more trend that you think is likely to stick around with NFTs. STEVE KACZYNSKI: Ooh. OK. I think what's called RWAs, or real-world assets, is one that I'm paying very close attention to. So if you have a Pokemon card, a Charizard card, or a Babe Ruth card as examples of things. Or my dad was a baseball collector, so those come to mind to me. He had Yankee Stadium seats and all these things. Right now, you can get certificates of authenticity, which you then put in like, what? Maybe a fireproof box under your bed, and you hope that it's safe. And maybe you can find it, maybe you can't. As we were looking through his stuff, some of them were in the back of the photo book. Some of them were in the back of the frame. Some of them were in a drawer somewhere. So the idea that you can authenticate on the actual blockchain a item that is a real-world asset-- and let's say that you don't even want to have it. I mean, there are people who buy art and vault it as an investment. If somebody wanted to do that, you could, let's say, have a Jackie Robinson card and have it vaulted through Brinks. There are companies working on this. And then have an exact digital representation of it, which is-- and people would say like, oh, well, the physical one, don't you want the physical one? Well, my kids, as they age into the consumer ages, they don't care as much about physical items. In fact, my daughter bought a Roblox plushy strictly to get the digital item so that she could flex it online in digital spaces, and nobody sees the physical plushy.
